summary.text: Cnidaria is a phylum of over 11,000 species of aquatic invertebrates, mostly marine, including jellyfish, sea anemones and corals.
They are marked by a simple nerve net spread through a gelatinous body and by cnidocytes, specialized cells used mainly for envenomation and capturing prey.
Most take one of two radially symmetrical body forms, swimming medusae or sessile polyps, each with a mouth surrounded by tentacles.

facts.label: Stinging cells
facts.value: Cnidocytes, used mainly to capture prey

facts.label: Body openings
facts.value: One opening for ingestion and excretion

items.prompt: A jellyfish pulses through the water. What makes its bell spring back to shape after each push?

options.label: A thick, springy mesoglea
A hard shell around the bell
A ring of bones at its edge
A gas-filled sac at its centre

items.explain: The mesoglea of medusae is thick and springy, so it returns to its original shape after muscles around the edge contract and squeeze water out.

items.prompt: A sea anemone swallows a small prey animal. Where does its waste leave the body?

options.label: Through a separate opening at the far end of the body
Out of the same opening it fed through
Through its tentacles
Through its stinging cells

items.explain: Cnidarians have only one opening for ingestion and excretion, so they have no separate mouth and anus.

items.prompt: What single feature sets cnidarians apart from every other animal group?

options.label: A body made of a single layer of cells
A skeleton of bone built around the mouth
Tentacles that are used only for swimming
Cells that fire harpoon-like structures, mainly to capture prey

items.explain: Cnidarians are distinguished from all other animals by having cnidocytes that fire harpoon-like structures.

items.prompt: A diver wants to see a reef built by reef-forming corals. Where should she go?

options.label: Warm, shallow marine waters
Cold polar waters
Deep, dark ocean water
A freshwater lake

items.explain: Reef-forming corals are almost entirely restricted to warm and shallow marine waters, while other cnidarians live at great depths, in polar regions and in freshwater.

items.prompt: Besides catching prey, how do many cnidarians get much of their nutrition?

options.label: By absorbing dissolved minerals from the seabed
Through a second mouth on the far end of the body
From symbiotic dinoflagellates living with them
By eating the stinging cells of other cnidarians

items.explain: Most cnidarians prey on other organisms, but many obtain much of their nutrition from symbiotic dinoflagellates, and a few are parasites.

items.prompt: Do the oldest cnidarian fossils come from before or after the Cambrian explosion?

options.label: After it, from rocks formed during the Ordovician radiation
Before it, from rocks about 580 million years old in the Ediacaran period
At the same time, because both began in the Cambrian
After it, since cnidarians appeared once corals diversified

items.explain: Cnidarian fossils have been found in rocks formed about 580 million years ago during the Ediacaran period, preceding the Cambrian Explosion.
